newsitem.title: USA: CSCE coffee rallies sharply, July sets new high.
newsitem.headline: CSCE coffee rallies sharply, July sets new high.

text.p: CSCE coffee futures exploded higher on Tuesday, with the benchmark July contract surging nearly seven percent, as continued concerns about the supply of quality arabica beans fueled a speculative-led rally, market sources said.

July arabicas shot up to a new life-of-contract high of 275.00 cents per lb before settling at 274.30 cents, up a whopping 17.45 cents on the day. Second-position September closed 11.45 cents higher, at 237.50 cents, while the back months rose 0.50 to 6.00.

"The perception is that supply is tight and will remain tight into the December contract," said Refco analyst Ann Prendergast. "I don't expect to see any enormous amount of coffee coming onto the market between now and October, and that's going to support prices."
Reflecting near-term supply worries, the July/September spread ballooned a hefty 6.00 cents from Friday's close, to 36.80 cents.
Arabica prices headed lower at the outset, as some weekend longs liquidated after top-grower Brazil got through the weekend without any crop-damaging cold weather, traders said.
But keen buying interest toward the lows and some roaster price-fixing stemmed losses and prompted disappointed locals to cover short positions, they said.
Upward momentum accelerated after the July contract pierced technical resistance at 262.00, the 265.00, triggering buy-stops.
Additionally, traders said the upswing was exaggerated by a lack of selling, with many Latin American origins believed to be well sold ahead of their 1997/98 harvest this fall.
"There are a lack of sellers in this market," a trader said. "Nothing is stopping it right now."

New York coffee futures have staged a blistering, uninterrupted rally since the end of last year. Prices have jumped by more than 150 percent as inventories in both consuming and producing countries hovered near 20-year lows.

Supply worries were exacerbated by forecasts for smaller-than-expected crops in many Latin American countries, labor unrest in Colombia and Brazil and projections for a smaller crop in Brazil in the coming 1997/98 season.

News from the Association of Coffee Producing Countries' meeting last week in London that 14-nation group agreed to continue to limit members' exports to 52.75 million bags for 12 months from July 1, re-ignited supply concerns.
In a bi-weekly report, Merrill Lynch analysts Judith Ganes said the accord by coffee producers to extend export curbs by a year, if honoured, would keep roaster stocks from rebuilding next season.

"The ACPC instead opted for the safe alternative and that was to extend the existing pact for one more year...If abided (by) the impact will keep consumer stocks from rebuilding next season," she said.

In addition to low inventory levels, traders said the market would be underpinned by the approach of the Brazilian winter, with any signs of cool weather likely to prompt jittery buying. Two severe frosts in 1994, one in June and another in July, damaged some of Brazil's coffee trees and sent world prices spinning higher.
"There is still a tightness in quality supplies of coffee," said Dean Witter analyst Steve Platt. "And an unwillingness to sell it in advance of the Brazilian winter."
On the July charts, traders are eyeing the 280.00-cent level, a 20-year high reached earlier this month on the now-expired May contract. The next upside objective was seen at 291.00 cents.

But while the market appears to be racing toward the $3 mark without looking back, some traders fear a consumer backlash in response to higher retail prices. Large roasters have already hiked prices on their 13-ounce can of regular ground coffee by nearly 50 percent, and traders said another increase -- the fifth -- could be in store for coffee drinkers in the next couple of weeks.

((--Patricia Avidan, New York Commodity Desk 212 859 1640))
